facts.label: legend
facts.quote: According to Hindu mythology, when Lord Shiva was going to Kashi along with one crore gods and goddesses he made a night halt at this location... Lord Shiva set out for Kashi himself cursing the others to become stone images.
facts.source_name: Tripura State Portal and Folklore Archives
facts.text: According to regional folklore, Lord Shiva was journeying to Kashi with an entourage of one crore deities when he cursed the remaining ninety-nine lakh ninety-nine thousand nine hundred ninety-nine into stone for failing to wake before sunrise.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: Another story revolves around one Kalu Kamar, the famous sculptor. He was assigned the task to build a crore of the deities in his dream. But keeping the last idol unfinished Kalu created his own image.
facts.text: A parallel regional legend attributes the site's rock carvings to an artisan named Kalu Kamar, who attempted to carve one crore divine statues in a single night to gain spiritual prestige but fell short by one image before daybreak.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The central Shiva head known as Unakotiswara Kal Bhairava is about 30 feet high including an embroidered head-dress which itself is 10 feet high.
facts.text: Archaeological surveys record that the central rock-cut Shiva head, designated Unakotiswara Kal Bhairava, stands approximately nine metres in height.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The bas relief sculptures at Unakoti are on stylistic grounds ascribed to 7th–9th century CE, to the period of Pre-Manikya rule.
facts.text: Stylistic analysis by archaeologists dates the primary rock-cut bas-relief sculptures of Unakoti between the seventh and ninth centuries CE.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Sculptures and rock-cut reliefs of the Unakotitirtha, Unakoti Range, N. Tripura.
facts.text: The Archaeological Survey of India officially classified the sculptures and rock-cut reliefs of Unakotitirtha as a centrally protected monument under its Aizawl Circle.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Rock-cut Sculptures and Reliefs of the Unakoti, Unakoti Range, Unakoti District... Date of Submission: 13/12/2022.
facts.text: The Archaeological Survey of India successfully proposed the rock-cut sculptures and reliefs of Unakoti for inclusion on the UNESCO World Heritage tentative list in the year 2022 CE.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The only inscription at Unakoti is on the other Chaturmukhalinga image, consisting of a couple of records in Bengali Characters of the 11th to 12th century CE, which mentions one Sri Jayadeva, probably a pilgrim.
facts.source_name: Epigraphia Indica / Archaeological Survey of India
facts.text: Epigraphic examination of a Chaturmukhalinga at Unakoti identified an inscription in medieval Bengali script dating to the twelfth century CE, referencing a pilgrim named Sri Jayadeva.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: The bas relief sculptures at Unakoti are on stylistic grounds ascribed to 7th–9th century CE, to the period of Pre-Manikya rule. The rock art was patronised by Deva Dynasty of Sribhumi in Samatata.
facts.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India / State Gazetteers
facts.text: Historians disagree regarding political patronage of the site, with some proposing the Deva dynasty of Samatata while others suggest pre-Manikya regional kings or Pala-period artistic workshops were responsible.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: According to the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), Unakoti dates back to the 8th or 9th century AD. Yet, many others differ with the opinion, conceding that it dates back longer further holding that those images were carved out in different spell of time.
facts.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India / Regional Academic Studies
facts.text: Scholars dispute whether the carvings were executed in a single concentrated phase during the early medieval era or added incrementally across multiple centuries lasting through the twelfth century CE.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: Unakoti literally means 'one less than one crore'... The site is a massive gallery set in a forested area displaying a number of towering low relief images.
facts.source_name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre / Archaeological Survey of India
facts.text: While traditional myth claims the hill holds exactly ninety-nine lakh ninety-nine thousand nine hundred ninety-nine sculptures, archaeological documentations have identified only several hundred rock reliefs and loose stone figures across the valley.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: A 15th generation descendant of King Jujhar Fa, a Shiva disciple who started the Tripurabda, prayed for Lord Shiva in a village called Chhambulnagar on the banks of the river Mau... assumed that the Chhambulnagar mentioned in Rajmala was situated near the Unakoti Hills.
facts.text: The Rajmala, the court chronicle of Tripura, describes early rulers performing worship of Lord Shiva along the Manu river in the territory historically identified with the Unakoti hills.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Among the rock-cut carvings, the central Shiva head and gigantic Ganesha figures deserve special mention.
facts.text: Archaeological fieldwork documents a prominent panel carved directly into the bed of the Unakoti hill stream containing three colossal depictions of Ganesha.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The site of Unakoti is located in the northeastern part of Tripura, about 8 km from Kailasahar and 185 km from the State capital Agartala.
facts.text: The archaeological complex of Unakoti is situated eight kilometres away from the subdivisional headquarters of Kailashahar in the state of Tripura.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: In the local Kokborok language, it is called Subrai Khung.
facts.source_name: Tripura State Tribal Cultural Research Institute
facts.text: Indigenous Kokborok tradition refers to the sacred site as Subrai Khung, honouring the local ancestral appellation for Shiva.
